Jebusites
JEB-yoo-sites
n. pl.
From Jebus, the old name of Jerusalem (Judges 19:10-11), itself from the personal name Jebus, third son of Canaan (Genesis 10:16). The Jebusites are the mountain people who held the ridge between the Kidron and the Tyropoeon valleys, and whose stronghold Israel could not take for four hundred years after Joshua.

Biblical Definition

The Jebusites are the people of Jebus, that is, of Jerusalem before it was Jerusalem. They stand in every list of the seven nations, and they are the standing monument to Israel’s unfinished obedience: the children of Judah could not drive them out (Joshua 15:63), and Benjamin did not either (Judges 1:21). For the whole period of the judges a Canaanite fortress sat in the middle of the inheritance, so unassailable that its garrison mocked David from the wall, saying the blind and the lame would keep him out (2 Samuel 5:6). Nevertheless David took the strong hold of Zion: the same is the city of David (2 Samuel 5:7). Then comes the turn that makes this entry more than military history. When David sinned in numbering Israel and the destroying angel stood over the city, the prophet Gad sent him to a Jebusite’s threshingfloor (2 Samuel 24:18). Araunah, called Ornan in Chronicles, offered his floor and his oxen freely; David refused to offer that which cost him nothing, and bought it. On that Jebusite threshingfloor Solomon built the house of the LORD (2 Chronicles 3:1). The last unconquered ground in Israel became the place of the altar, and then of the temple, and it is called mount Moriah.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 does not carry a separate JEBUSITE entry; the 1828 lexicon treats such gentilics under the general rule for proper nouns derived from a founder’s name, as it does with Canaanite.

expand to see more

JEBUSITE, n. — A descendant of Jebus, the third son of Canaan; an inhabitant of Jebus, afterward Jerusalem.

The name of the city survives in Judges 19:10, Jebus, which is Jerusalem, and in 1 Chronicles 11:4.

Webster’s treatment of biblical gentilics is uniformly genealogical and geographical; the theological freight is left to the text.

The English form follows the Vulgate Jebusaeus through Wycliffe and Tyndale into the Authorized Version.

Where 1828 is silent, the King James translators are not: they render the term consistently across some forty occurrences, which is itself a lexical service.

Key Scripture

Joshua 15:63 — "As for the Jebusites the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the children of Judah could not drive them out: but the Jebusites dwell with the children of Judah at Jerusalem unto this day."

Judges 1:21 — "And the children of Benjamin did not drive out the Jebusites that inhabited Jerusalem; but the Jebusites dwell with the children of Benjamin in Jerusalem unto this day."

2 Samuel 5:7 — "Nevertheless David took the strong hold of Zion: the same is the city of David."

2 Samuel 24:18 — "And Gad came that day to David, and said unto him, Go up, rear an altar unto the LORD in the threshingfloor of Araunah the Jebusite."

2 Chronicles 3:1 — "Then Solomon began to build the house of the LORD at Jerusalem in mount Moriah, where the LORD appeared unto David his father, in the place that David had prepared in the threshingfloor of Ornan the Jebusite."

Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a tolerated remnant of sin does not stay quiet, and that God nevertheless plants His altar on the very ground His people failed to take.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. What needs recovering is the plain sense of Joshua 15:63 and Judges 1:21, two verses that record a failure and then repeat, twice, the phrase unto this day. The Holy Ghost has the chronicler note that the compromise outlived the generation that made it. Incomplete obedience is not a lesser obedience; it is a standing arrangement with what God said to remove, and it endures long after the men who arranged it are dead. Every pastor knows the domestic version of this: the sin not put to death in youth still holds its ridge in middle age, and its garrison still taunts from the wall.

The second thing to recover is the astonishing end of the story. God did not merely give David the fortress; He directed the altar to the threshingfloor of a Jebusite, and there Solomon raised the temple. The ground of longest resistance became the ground of atonement, and mount Moriah is where Abraham had already been told that God would provide Himself a lamb. Grace does not merely forgive the failure; it takes the very site of it and builds the house of sacrifice on it. That is the pattern of the gospel in a plot of threshing ground, and David’s refusal to offer that which doth cost me nothing is the right response to it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Yebusi (H2983), the Jebusite, from Yebus (H2982), Jebus — a name connected with the root bus, to tread down, fitting for both a threshingfloor and a trodden city.

expand to see more

Hebrew Yebus (H2982) — Jebus, the ancient name of Jerusalem (Judges 19:10; 1 Chronicles 11:4).

Hebrew Yebusi (H2983) — Jebusite; the gentilic used some forty times from Genesis 10:16 to Zechariah 9:7.

Hebrew bus (H947) — to tread down, to trample; the likely root behind the name.

Hebrew goren (H1637) — threshingfloor; Araunah’s floor in 2 Samuel 24:18 and the temple site of 2 Chronicles 3:1.

Araunah (2 Samuel 24) and Ornan (1 Chronicles 21) are the same man under two spellings, a common feature of the parallel histories.

Usage

"The children of Judah could not drive them out (Joshua 15:63) — the honest record of an unfinished conquest."

"Nevertheless David took the strong hold of Zion (2 Samuel 5:7) — four centuries late, but taken."

"In the threshingfloor of Ornan the Jebusite (2 Chronicles 3:1) — the last Canaanite ground becomes the temple mount."
